details:
**Symphonie fantastique**
Berlioz's 1830 five-movement program symphony, subtitled "Episode in the Life of an Artist." A young artist poisons himself with opium out of hopeless love and has a series of visions: "Reveries – Passions," "A Ball" (a waltz with two harps), "Scene in the Fields," "March to the Scaffold," and "Dream of a Witches' Sabbath." Franz Liszt transcribed it for piano. Berlioz's sequel, the monodrama Lélio, or The Return to Life, follows the artist after he survives.

**Idée fixe**
The recurring melody that represents the beloved woman in every movement of the Symphonie fantastique. It is often played by the clarinet and is transformed each time, most famously into a shrill, grotesque E-flat clarinet tune in the finale. The term ("fixed idea") is Berlioz's own.

**Harriet Smithson**
The Irish Shakespearean actress whom Berlioz fell obsessively in love with after seeing her as Ophelia and Juliet in Paris. She inspired the Symphonie fantastique, and they later married.

**"March to the Scaffold"**
The fourth movement of the Symphonie fantastique, in which the artist dreams he has killed his beloved and is led to his execution. It opens with muffled timpani, and the idée fixe is cut off by the guillotine's fall, after which pizzicato notes depict the severed head rolling, followed by loud G major chords.

**"Dream of a Witches' Sabbath"**
The finale of the Symphonie fantastique, in which the artist sees himself at a hellish gathering of witches. Funeral bells introduce a parody of the Gregorian chant Dies irae, which is then combined with the witches' round dance.

**"Scene in the Fields"**
The third movement of the Symphonie fantastique. An onstage English horn and an offstage oboe play a ranz des vaches (shepherd's call) back and forth, and at the end four timpanists depict distant thunder while the English horn calls with no reply.

**Harold in Italy**
Berlioz's second symphony (1834), inspired by Lord Byron's Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, with a solo viola representing Harold. Its movements include "Harold in the Mountains," a "Serenade" of an Abruzzi mountaineer, and the "Orgy of the Brigands." Niccolò Paganini commissioned it but refused to play it because the viola part was not virtuosic enough; he later rewarded Berlioz generously.

**Requiem (Grande Messe des morts)**
Berlioz's huge 1837 Requiem, written for enormous forces including 16 timpani and a large chorus. In the "Tuba mirum," four offstage brass bands placed at the four compass points enter. It also contains a "Lacrymosa" in 9/8 and an "Offertorium" subtitled "Chorus of Souls in Purgatory," in which the chorus sings only the notes A and B-flat. According to Berlioz, the conductor Habeneck stopped to take snuff during the premiere and Berlioz took over.

**The Damnation of Faust**
Berlioz's "dramatic legend," a hybrid of opera and oratorio based on Goethe's Faust. Famous orchestral excerpts include the "Ballet of the Sylphs" and the "Dance of the Will-o'-the-Wisps." In Auerbach's tavern, Brander sings a song about a poisoned rat, and Faust's aria "Nature immense, impénétrable et fière" asks Nature to relieve his despair.

**Rákóczi March**
A Hungarian march, opening with a trumpet fanfare, that Berlioz orchestrated and placed in The Damnation of Faust, moving Faust to the plains of Hungary so that he could include it.

**Treatise on Instrumentation and Orchestration**
Berlioz's influential 1844 book describing the instruments of the orchestra and how to use them. It defines an instrument as "any sounding body used by a composer." Berlioz also orchestrated Carl Maria von Weber's piano piece Invitation to the Dance, which opens with a solo cello.

**Roméo et Juliette**
Berlioz's "dramatic symphony" based on Shakespeare's play, combining orchestral movements with chorus and solo voices. Its "Queen Mab" scherzo uses antique cymbals (crotales), and the finale ends with Friar Laurence, a bass, leading the families in an "Oath of Reconciliation" in B major.

**Benvenuto Cellini and the Roman Carnival Overture**
Benvenuto Cellini is Berlioz's opera about the Florentine sculptor of Perseus with the Head of Medusa, who must finish a commission for Pope Clement VII. Cellini accidentally kills Pompeo and escapes in a monk's disguise. Berlioz reused its music in the Roman Carnival Overture, where the English horn plays a love song from the opera before a fast saltarello takes over.

**Les Troyens (The Trojans)**
Berlioz's grand opera based on Virgil's Aeneid. In the first part, the Trojan women led by Cassandra choose mass suicide rather than be captured by the Greeks; the second part follows Aeneas and Dido at Carthage.

**Les nuits d'été (Summer Nights)**
A song cycle setting six poems by Théophile Gautier, originally for voice and piano and later orchestrated by Berlioz.
